title: Americans Are Ditching Multivitamins for Targeted Supplements — and Two of the Fastest-Growing Are Ayurvedic Staples
excerpt: A 25-year JAMA analysis of 63,000 adults finds supplement use surging while multivitamin use drops — with turmeric and ashwagandha leading the charge
body:
Americans are taking more supplements than ever — but they're increasingly skipping the all-in-one multivitamin in favour of targeted pills they believe will address specific health goals. A sweeping new analysis published in *JAMA Network Open*, spanning 25 years of national dietary data, reveals a quiet but significant shift in how the country thinks about daily health.

The study, led by researchers at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center and the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, analysed supplement use data from more than 63,000 U.S. adults between 1999 and 2023. Overall supplement use rose from 51% to 60% of the adult population, with the sharpest jump — from 62% to 78% — among adults aged 65 and older.

But here's the catch: multivitamin use actually *declined*, from 35% to 31%, over the same period. What surged instead were individual supplements — vitamin D, zinc, magnesium, vitamin B12, and turmeric, along with newer entrants like ashwagandha, collagen, probiotics, and elderberry.

## The Longevity Movement Meets Ayurveda

The trend reflects a broader cultural shift toward precision wellness. Rather than trusting a single pill to cover all bases, consumers are curating supplement stacks tailored to specific concerns: immune support, gut health, inflammation, skin and joint health. The post-pandemic era accelerated this, with zinc and vitamin D seeing the steepest climbs as immune anxiety lingered.

For the Indian diaspora, the data carries a familiar undertone. Turmeric and ashwagandha — two of the fastest-growing supplements in the American market — are foundational to Ayurvedic medicine, a system of traditional healing that millions of South Asian families grew up with. What Western wellness influencers are now marketing as cutting-edge, many NRI households have kept in their kitchen cabinets for generations.

"The rise in supplement use aligns with the longevity movement, as more people seek products tailored to specific health goals," the researchers noted. But they were careful to add a caveat: the study shows that people are *taking* more supplements, not that these supplements are *effective* for the conditions they're being used for.

## What the Evidence Actually Says

That distinction matters. A 2024 analysis of nearly 400,000 U.S. adults, led by the National Cancer Institute and published in the same journal, found no association between regular multivitamin use and a lower risk of death from any cause — including cancer or heart disease. A separate Cochrane review reached similar conclusions for most individual supplements.

Vitamin D is an exception: evidence supports its role in bone health and potentially immune function, and the study found it to be one of the most commonly added supplements. Magnesium, too, has growing research backing for heart health and sleep quality. But for many trending supplements — collagen for skin, ashwagandha for stress, elderberry for colds — the evidence remains either preliminary or mixed.

The supplement industry in the United States is now worth over $60 billion annually, and it's largely unregulated compared to pharmaceuticals. The FDA does not require manufacturers to prove efficacy before selling a supplement, only that the product is safe and accurately labelled.

## Why NRIs Should Pay Attention

For South Asians in the U.S., Canada, and the UK, the supplement question intersects with a broader health reality. The diaspora faces elevated risks for type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and vitamin D deficiency — the last one partly due to darker skin producing less vitamin D from sunlight at higher latitudes.

A targeted vitamin D supplement may genuinely make sense for many NRIs, particularly those in northern climates. Magnesium, too, is worth discussing with a physician, given its role in blood sugar regulation — a concern for a population with high diabetes prevalence.

But the broader lesson from this research is one of caution. The shift from multivitamins to targeted supplements isn't inherently better or worse — it's just different marketing meeting consumer demand. Without rigorous clinical evidence, many of these products remain expensive placebos at best.

The smartest approach, as multiple experts have noted, remains the least profitable one: a balanced diet rich in whole foods, regular movement, and a conversation with your doctor before adding any pill to the routine.

*Sources: JAMA Network Open (June 2026), Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, National Cancer Institute (JAMA Network Open, 2024)*
